'''''Muehlenbeckia complexa''''' is a plant commonly known as '''''pohuehue''''' ({{langx|mi|pōhuehue}}), although this name also applies to some other climbers such as ''[[Muehlenbeckia australis]]''.<ref>Poole, Alec Lindsay (1966). [http://www.TeAra.govt.nz/en/1966/pohuehue/1 Pohuehue], from ''An Encyclopaedia of New Zealand'', edited by A. H. McLintock, originally published in 1966. Te Ara - the Encyclopedia of New Zealand. Updated 22 April 2009.</ref>

==Description==
''Muehlenbeckia complexa'' is one of 50 species of shrubs that are divided into 21 family groups known to be [[divaricate]], with interlaced branches and a reduced number of leaves. This trait is more or less unique to [[New Zealand]], with very few divaricate species being found elsewhere in the world.<ref>Went, F. (1971). Parallel Evolution. Taxon, 20(2/3), 197-226. doi:10.2307/1218877</ref> ''M. complexa'' is a vascular [[Native species|native]] of New Zealand,  belonging to the [[Polygonaceae]] family.<ref>New Zealand plant conservation network. (n.d) Muehlenbeckia complexa var. Complexa. Available from https://www.nzpcn.org.nz/flora/species/muehlenbeckia-complexa-var-complexa/?download=pdfWent, F. (1971). Parallel Evolution. Taxon, 20(2/3), 197-226. doi:10.2307/1218877</ref> ''M. complexa'' forms a dense thick mass of interlaced branches.  The stems are slender and creep or twine over other plants or rocks, without support it will climb upon itself.  Forming thick and dense prostrate masses.  When it occurs near the shore, frequently assumes cushion form.<ref>Cockayne, L. (1927). New Zealand plants and their story. W. A. G. Skinner, Government printer.</ref> The stems are tough and woody, with numerous branches  tightly interlaced, bark is red-brown in colour and have a wiry appearance.  The leaves are petiolate, variable in shape and size, even on the same plant.<ref name="Cheeseman">Cheeseman, F. T (1925) Manual of New Zealand flora. W. A. G. Skinner, Government printer</ref> Leaves may have lobed or entire margins.  The leaves are rather sparse on slender stalks, up to 1 cm long, the leaf blade ranges from 5mm to 20 cm long by 2 to 15mm long.  The flowers are delightfully scented and are supported on spikes approximately 2 cm long, that emerge from the leaf axils and the tips of branchlets.  The flowers are small, [[dioecious]] and contain 8 stamens.<ref name="Cheeseman"/> As the flowers age, they enlarge into succulent fruits that are semi transparent with a shiny, black, triangular shaped seeds located in the centre of the fruits.  It is [[semi-deciduous]], losing most, or all of its leaves over winter.<ref name="Metcalf">Metcalf. L. (2009). Know your New Zealand native plants. New Holland publishers (NZ)</ref>

=== Other names ===
Other names include {{lang|mi|tororaro}} ([[Māori language|Māori]]), mattress plant, wiggy-bush,<ref name="Metcalf"/> and
wire vine.<ref name="Clark">Clarke, A. (2007). The great sacred forest of Tane. Reed publishing (NZ)</ref>
Commonly known as maidenhair vine, creeping wire vine, lacy wire vine, angel vine, mattress vine, mattress wire weed, necklace vine, and wire vine, ''Muehlenbeckia complexa'' is an [[ornamental plant]] in the family [[Polygonaceae]], which is native to [[New Zealand]].<ref name="Pink 2004">{{cite book | author=Pink, A. | url=https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/11892|title=Gardening for the Million| year=2004 | publisher=[[Project Gutenberg|Project Gutenberg Literary Archive Foundation]]}}</ref> 
It got its genus name after botanist [[Muehlenbeck]], and earned its species name due to its tangled growth habit.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.nzpcn.org.nz/flora_details.aspx?ID=991|title=Muehlenbeckia complexa var. complexa {{!}} New Zealand Plant Conservation Network|website=www.nzpcn.org.nz|access-date=2019-05-10}}</ref>

== Distribution and habitat ==
It can be found growing throughout all three main islands of [[New Zealand]] (as well as [[Lord Howe Island]] in Australia), where it grows in a variety of habitats, occurring in coastal, lowland and montane regions. ''M. complexa'' is often found growing in company of ''[[Plagianthus divaricatus]]'', shore ribbonwood.<ref name="Metcalf"/>

Common throughout both Eastern and Western coasts of the United States including Hawaii, and native to New Zealand. This plant has also been introduced in Western Australia,<ref name="Florabase">{{FloraBase|name=Muehlenbeckia complexa|id=16896}}</ref> Mexico, the United Kingdom, Malaysia, Japan, and parts of South America.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://inaturalist.nz/taxa/78126-Muehlenbeckia-complexa|title=Scrambling pohuehue (Muehlenbeckia complexa)|website=iNaturalist NZ|language=en|access-date=2019-05-10}}</ref>

Preferred climates are coastal regions.

==Ecology==
In its native environment it plays a key role sealing human and natural disturbances on the forest edge. It also suppresses the growth of introduced weeds, such as blackberry, and promotes increased insect diversity.<ref>[http://www.openspace.org.nz/Site/Managing_your_covenant/Restoration_information/muehlenbeckia.aspx Muehlenbeckia australis - A smothering cloak or a haven of biodiversity?] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180207175421/http://www.openspace.org.nz/Site/Managing_your_covenant/Restoration_information/muehlenbeckia.aspx |date=2018-02-07 }} Open Space Magazine No. 66, March 2006. QEII National Trust.</ref>

=== Ecological value for wildlife ===
A wide variety of insect species are associated with ''M. complexa''.<ref name="Crowe">Crowe, A. (2009). Which native forest plant? Penguin books (NZ)</ref> It is an important host plant for several [[endemic]] species of copper butterflies including the coastal copper (''[[Lycaena salustius]]'')<ref>Maanaki Whenua Landcare Research. (n.d) Copper butterfly. Retrieved from https://www.landcareresearch.co.nz/resources/identification/animals/bug-id/what-is-this-bug/bugs-with-legs/6-legs/moths-and-butterflies/copper-butterfly</ref> and Maui's copper (''[[Lycaena edna]]'').<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Henderson |first=Geoff |last2=Patrick |first2=Brian |year=2020 |title=New Zealand’s pōhuehue (Muehlenbeckia) - a biodiversity powerhouse with an image problem |url=https://bts.nzpcn.org.nz/site/assets/files/23402/canterbury_botanical_society_2020_journal_51_47-57.pdf |journal=Canterbury Botanical Society |issue=51 |pages=47-57}}</ref> ''M. complexa'' also hosts ''Aphis cotteri'', an aphid native to New Zealand,<ref>Bowie, M. (2001). Restoration of Quail Island invertebrates. Retrieved from http://dspace.lincoln.ac.nz/bitstream/handle/10182/723/wmr_22.pdf?sequence=4&isAllowed=y {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230402100846/https://dspace.lincoln.ac.nz/bitstream/handle/10182/723/wmr_22.pdf?sequence=4&isAllowed=y |date=2023-04-02 }}</ref> the pohuehue gall moth (''Morova subfasciata'')<ref name="Crowe"/> and an endemic mite known as the pohuehue pocket gall mite (''Eriophyes lambi'').<ref>Martin. N. A. (2017). Pohuehue pocket gall mite - Eriophyes lambi. Retrieved from https://nzacfactsheets.landcareresearch.co.nz/factsheet/InterestingInsects/Pohuehue-pocket-gall-mite---Eriophyes-lambi.htm</ref> It is also a food source for birds such as [[tūī]], [[New Zealand bellbird|bellbird]] and [[kererū]],<ref name="Crowe"/> which also feed on the buds and leaves.<ref name="Crowe"/>

=== Predators, parasites, and diseases ===
[[Australian brush-tailed possum|Possums]] will readily eat ''Muehlenbeckia'' species.<ref name="Crowe"/>

=== Other information ===
Since 1995 or earlier, it has been a problematic invasive species in the [[Golden Gate National Recreation Area]]<ref>[http://www.ice.ucdavis.edu/nrpi/NRPIDescription.asp?ProjectPK=4786 Mattress Wire Weed Control in Golden Gate National Recreational Area]{{Dead link|date=June 2025 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref> including [[Lands End, San Francisco]]<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.cal-ipc.org/symposia/archive/pdf/2006/06ObscureDG.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161026233732/https://www.cal-ipc.org/symposia/archive/pdf/2006/06ObscureDG.pdf |title=2006 Cal-IPC Symposium  |author=Obscure Weeds Discussion Group |archive-date=2016-10-26}}</ref> and the [[Presidio of San Francisco]]<ref>[http://www.mayandassociatesinc.com/index.asp?pgid=29 Habitat Restoration Projects: Mattress Wire Weed Control Study, The Presidio Trust of San Francisco] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20050422122951/http://www.mayandassociatesinc.com/index.asp?pgid=29 |date=2005-04-22 }}</ref> and eradication requires 3–5 years monitoring and maintenance.<ref>[http://www.ci.sf.ca.us/site/uploadedfiles/bdsupvrs/leganalyst/OLA_096-06_Natural_Area_Mgmt_Plans_final.pdf San Francisco Board of Supervisors Legislative Analyst Report, Natural Areas Management Plans, July 2, 2007] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081114125131/http://www.ci.sf.ca.us/site/uploadedfiles/bdsupvrs/leganalyst/OLA_096-06_Natural_Area_Mgmt_Plans_final.pdf |date=November 14, 2008 }}</ref> Uncontrolled maidenhair vines can overrun gardens, climb trees and choke other plants.
[[image:Uncontrolled maidenhair vine.jpg|thumb|Uncontrolled maidenhair vine]]

==Cultural uses==
The succulent flowers were eaten by [[Māori people|Māori]], especially children as they are sweet and juicy.<ref name="Clark"/>
